system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2182-05-23 15:18:00 to 2182-05-26 14:35:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with stage IV cholangiocarcinoma and biliary stents, was admitted with a fever of 101.2°F and night sweats, following a recent chemotherapy cycle. He had no localizing symptoms, and evaluation showed no evidence of infection. Chest X-ray revealed no acute process, and abdominal ultrasound showed stable biliary ductal dilation and gallbladder sludge without signs of obstruction. Liver enzymes were mildly elevated, but bilirubin remained normal. Blood cultures were negative at 48 hours, and he remained afebrile after initial presentation. Antibiotics were discontinued, and he was discharged home in stable condition with plans to continue outpatient oncology care.
problems: Fever, unspecified
Malignant neoplasm of intrahepatic bile ducts
Hypertrophy (benign) of prostate without urinary obstruction and other lower urinary tract symptom (LUTS)
Migraine, unspecified, without mention of intractable migraine without mention of status migrainosus
Allergy, unspecified, not elsewhere classified
Sleep disturbance, unspecified

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you've been having fevers and feeling unwell. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had chills and a fever for a couple of days. I felt really weak and my skin looked a bit yellow again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your bilirubin is elevated, which explains the jaundice. Given your history of cholangiocarcinoma and biliary stents, we’re concerned about a possible blockage or infection in your bile ducts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I’m here? Because of the stents getting blocked again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ve ordered an ultrasound and blood tests. The ultrasound shows your stents are in place, but there’s sludge and mild thickening, which could be contributing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens now? Do I need another procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning an ERCP tomorrow. It’s a procedure to look inside your bile ducts, clear any blockages, and make sure the stents are working properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt? I remember the last one wasn’t too bad, but I was sedated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be under monitored anesthesia, so you’ll be comfortable and won’t feel anything. The team will explain everything before you go in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. And the antibiotics I’m on now—will they help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started you on IV antibiotics—cefepime and metronidazole—to treat possible infection. Once we clear the blockage, we may switch to an oral antibiotic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my liver numbers—they’re high again, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your bilirubin and liver enzymes are elevated, which fits with a bile duct issue. We expect them to improve after the ERCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my chemotherapy? I was supposed to get my next dose soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve held your gemcitabine and cisplatin for now. It’s safer to wait until the infection is under control. We’ll reschedule it for next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I just don’t want the cancer to progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not expecting that. This is a manageable complication. Your oncology team will make sure you get back on track quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. Your blood cultures came back negative, which is reassuring—no bacteria in your bloodstream.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. So it’s not a serious infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s cholangitis—an infection in the bile ducts caused by blockage. But since we caught it early and you’re responding to antibiotics, it’s treatable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the ERCP is still on for today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s scheduled for noon. The team will remove any sludge or debris and may place a new stent to keep things draining well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. Johnson. You did great during the ERCP. We cleared both stents—there was a lot of sludge, pus, and even some tumor tissue blocking them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds intense. Did you fix the blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We placed a new plastic stent in the main duct and left hepatic duct. The right metal stent was cleaned out with balloon sweeps. Drainage looks excellent now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another procedure soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need a follow-up ERCP in six weeks to remove the new plastic stent. The metal ones can stay longer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching from IV to oral ciprofloxacin—500 mg twice a day for five days. Much easier for you now that you’re improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs are looking better—bilirubin is down from 2.5 to 1.4, and liver enzymes are improving. You’re afebrile now, which is great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better too. No more chills or fatigue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly what we want to see. We’ll keep monitoring, but you’re on track for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I go back to my normal diet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve advanced you to a regular diet. Just take it easy on fatty foods—they can be harder to digest with your condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your labs continue to improve, and you’ve had no fever since yesterday. We’re ready to discharge you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish the ciprofloxacin, watch for fever, abdominal pain, or jaundice. If any of those happen, call your doctor or come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have an ERCP in six weeks to remove the plastic stent. Your oncologist will also reschedule your chemotherapy next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with stage IV cholangiocarcinoma and biliary stents, was admitted with fever, chills, and elevated bilirubin. Imaging showed stent obstruction with sludge and pus, leading to cholangitis. He underwent an ERCP where both stents were cleared, and a new plastic stent was placed. His liver function improved, fevers resolved, and he was switched to oral antibiotics. Chemotherapy was held during admission and rescheduled. He was discharged home in stable condition with plans for stent removal in six weeks and resumed oncology care.
